You're designing a part for someone to 3D print at home. They'll print it on their own printer, use only the hardware listed below, and put it together by following your manual.

## Their setup
- Printer: Bambu Lab X1C (with AMS), build volume 256 x 256 x 256 mm
- Nozzle: 0.4 mm
- Layer height: 0.2 mm
- Filament: PLA (high-speed PLA, black)
- Longest bridge seen to print cleanly on this setup: 50 mm

## Hardware they can use
Refer to an item by its catalog reference: "ISO 4762 M5x30" (socket head screw, size x length, from the lengths listed), "ISO 4032 M5" (hex nut), "ISO 10511 M5" (nylon-insert lock nut), "ISO 7089 M5" (washer), "ASME B18.2.2 1/4-20" (1/4"-20 nut), "insert M3x4x5" (heat-set insert), "salvaged:webcam-mount-bolt".

## How to work
You have these tools:
- measure(item, what): ask the person to measure one of their own things, such as their desk or their phone. They answer with what they measured, or say they can't measure it.
- submit_design(...): hand in the finished design. This ends the conversation.
- report_limitation(wanted, blocked_by, why): say you wanted to use something (a technique, a tool, a part or material, a way of handing in the design) but couldn't because of what's available here. It doesn't change anything, but it's noted.
You have at most 8 turns. Hand in a design before they run out.

## The design you hand in
submit_design's schema describes every field. The rules that matter:
- Every dimension that comes from hardware or the real world is a named param, with its source: measured (the person measured it for you), datasheet, catalog, asked (the person told you), guessed, unknown, or design (your own choice).
- Each part's `code` is Python that defines build(p) and returns a CadQuery Workplane or Shape. `cq` is already imported, and p.<name> is each param's value. Dimensions that come from hardware or the real world must come from params.
- Model each part in the orientation it's printed in, with z = 0 on the bed.
- The manual is the steps the person follows, naming the parts and hardware each step uses.

I'm starting on a robot arm, and the first joint is an MG996R servo. Could I 3D print a plate that holds the servo with its shaft sticking up? It should screw on through the servo's mounting tabs and sit firm, with no wobble. I'll work out how the plate fixes to the base later. I've got the servo here, and the screws, nuts and washers on your list.

Measurements I took:
- servo body length: 40.58 mm (the case, end to end, not counting the tabs)
- servo body width: 19.82 mm (the case, side to side)
- servo body height: 40.4 mm (the case, top to bottom)
- servo tab holes: 4.58 mm (each mounting tab has two holes, open to the tab's end like a U)
- servo hole spacing: 44.61 mm (between the holes on the two tabs, from the inside edge of one to the inside edge of the other; I didn't measure the spacing between the two holes on one tab)
- servo tab thickness: 2.28 mm
- servo tab to top: 5.63 to 5.69 mm (from the top face of a tab (the shaft side) to the top of the case)
- servo rib width: 1.51 mm (a rib on each tab's top face (the shaft side), between the tab's two holes; it stops the tabs sitting flush)
- servo rib height: 1.8 mm (how far the rib stands up from the tab's top face)
- servo rib position: 8.31 mm (from the side of the holes to the middle of the rib)
- servo cable exit: out of one end of the case, below the tabs (where the cable leaves; I didn't measure its size or how far it sticks out)

reasoning:
I'm working out how the servo sits in the plate: it drops through a rectangular cutout, and the tab bottoms rest on the plate's top surface since the ribs are on top. The screws then run down through the tab holes and the plate, with nuts underneath.

I'm checking whether the head and washer would clear the rib between the two holes, since the rib sits on the top face. The numbers are unclear, with the rib position and hole spacing not matching the standard dimensions I'd expect, so I'm trying a few interpretations to see which fits.

I'm checking whether a washer on top would clear the rib, and it wouldn't, so the washer goes under the nut instead. Since the rib sits at the centerline, I also want to confirm the hole spacing and see whether an M4 screw leaves enough room.

I'm now thinking about the cable, which exits below the tabs at one end, so the cutout needs a notch in that end wall to let it through. I'm also checking the hole spacing: 44.61 mm between the inner edges plus a 4.58 mm hole gives about 49.19 mm center to center, close to the nominal figure. I still want to measure the spacing within one tab and the size of the cable exit.

I'm thinking about the tab layout now: the ribs sit on top, so the nut pockets go on the underside where they can capture the nut. I still want the spacing between the two holes on one tab, the cable exit distance below the tabs, and the overall tab length, which seems to be about 54 mm on a 70 x 40 plate.

I'm sizing the screw length now: with an 8 mm plate and the nut sitting 3.5 mm down in its pocket, an M4x12 screw would stick out about 1.7 mm below the plate, so I need to check whether a shorter screw fits better.

I'm sizing the screw length against the plate: an M4x12 would poke about 1.7 mm past the bottom, so I'll try an M4x10 instead, which leaves the tip just under the bottom face. With a 4 mm nut pocket, the nut sits fully engaged and the screw tip ends a little past the nut.

I'm picking the nut retention next: a plain M4 hex nut, which fits the 4 mm pocket depth and is enough since the screws stay clamped.

I'm planning to check the spacing between the two holes on one tab and the cable exit height below the tab underside, since the cable-notch sizing depends on both. I'll also make a small test coupon of the cutout and holes to verify the fit before printing the full plate.

reasoning:
I can't measure the rib directly, so I'm using the rib's position instead, taken as the distance from the side of the holes to the middle of the rib, which is 8.31. I'm not sure whether the rib runs across the width or along the length, so I'm working out which axis that distance lies on. If the rib sits centered between two holes, the hole center would be 8.31 minus 2.29 from that reference point.

I'm working out the hole spacing from the rib's distance, which gives about 12 mm against the datasheet's 10 mm, so I'm treating the holes as slots across the width to cover that range. I'll widen the nut pocket to match and check the fit against the M4 head and the rib width, and I'll add a cable notch at one end of the cutout.

I'm checking whether a 12 mm notch at the end of the plate would collide with the hole area, since the holes sit about 24.6 mm from center and the body ends around 20.3 mm. The cable likely exits a few millimeters above the case bottom, so the 8 mm plate probably clears it, but I'm still unsure how high the cable actually comes out and whether the servo can be lowered through the cutout with the cable attached.

I'm picturing the cable exiting near the bottom of the end face, so a small notch might be needed for the grommet to pass during insertion. I'm considering a notch about 7 mm wide and 4 mm deep past the body end, but I still need to check whether its edge overlaps the hole area.

I'm trying to pin down where the notch can sit without running into the nut pockets, since the pockets reach down through the full plate height and a through-cut notch would overlap them. I'm weighing whether to shift the nuts or narrow the notch, and whether a shallower cut in only part of the plate could still let the grommet pass.

I'm considering flipping the approach: the servo could go in from below, with its tabs under the plate and the case and shaft poking up through the cutout. That would keep the cable below the tabs, so it never has to pass through the plate, and grooves for the ribs could stop the servo flush against the underside.

I'm weighing the screw setup from underneath: M4 screws come up through the tabs into the plate, with nuts and washers on top, and the 4 mm plate leaves room for a short M4x12 screw.

I'm checking whether the screw heads fit below the tabs, and they do since they sit outboard of the body. The plate would hang the servo from its underside, which is a common base layout, though it leaves the screws in tension. The ribs stand on the tab tops, so grooves in the plate would be needed to seat them, and I'm trying to size those.

I'm checking the groove along the underside: a 2.0 mm wide, 2.1 mm deep channel on the centerline running from the body end out to the plate edge, which should seat the rib. Since the plate prints with its underside on the bed, the groove stays open and needs no support, and the nuts sit on top. I'm also comparing the cutout against the case top footprint, which looks the same, so a 0.2 mm clearance per side should locate the servo snugly.

I'm checking the hole-to-cutout wall next, which comes out to about 1.9 mm, so that works. Since the shaft pokes through the plate and the case stands about 1.6 mm above it, the horn should clear. I'm now wondering whether a groove along the centerline under the tabs will be needed.

I'm settling on a 5 mm plate, since it's stiffer and still leaves the case top just barely above it, so the horn can clear. Next I'm checking the screw stack-up: tab, plate, washer, and nut come to about 11.3 mm, which means the M4x12 screw would only protrude slightly past the nut.

I'm weighing whether to put the screws in from underneath with M4x12 and no washer under the head, since a longer screw would poke up near the horn, and I'm checking whether the tabs still give enough bearing surface.

I'm settling the fastener layout: heads go on top of the plate with a washer beneath, and the nut sits under the tab with a washer, which spreads the load across the U-slot better. That stacks up to about 12 mm, so an M4x16 screw works, with its tip sticking out below the plate.

I'm settling the lock nut and screw lengths, and the M4x16 still clears the nut. Next I'm sizing the slot to 4.5 mm for screw clearance, then fixing the hole spacing and the underside groove, which runs out to the plate edge.

I'm deciding on a 70 by 40 mm plate and weighing whether to make a 3 mm thick test coupon with the same cutout, slots, and rib groove, since the 2.2 mm groove needs at least that much thickness.
